name: Losar
summary: Losar, the Tibetan new year, is the biggest family festival of the year for the Lachungpas and Lachenpas, whose roots are Tibetan. It is marked at home and in the gompas with prayers, offerings, new clothes and visits, at the coldest time of year.
body: Losar falls on the first day of the first month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in February and sometimes early March. Across Sikkim it is celebrated by communities of Tibetan heritage, and in the high villages of Lachung and Lachen, where most families trace their roots across the passes, it is the main holiday of the winter. Preparations begin days earlier with house cleaning and special food.

The festival is mostly private and religious. Families visit the monastery to make offerings and light butter lamps, hang new prayer flags and spend the first days visiting relatives. Some hotels and shops close or run on reduced staff for a few days. For visitors, this means a quieter village and, if you are lucky, an invitation to tea.

Losar comes at the snowiest time of year, when the road to Lachung can close after fresh falls and Zero Point is usually shut. If you plan a snow trip around Losar, keep spare days in Gangtok, confirm that your hotel is open over the holiday and check current status before you travel.
tips: Confirm your Lachung hotel is open over Losar, as some family hotels close.
Visit the Lachung Monastery in the morning, dress modestly and walk clockwise.
Bring a khada scarf or small gift if you are invited into a home.

faqs.a: Losar follows the Tibetan lunar calendar, so the date moves each year, usually falling in February or early March. Check the published Tibetan calendar or ask your Sikkim operator once the date is announced. Sikkim usually declares a holiday for it. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How is Losar celebrated in Lachung
faqs.a: Mostly at home and in the monastery: cleaning houses, preparing special food, making offerings and lighting butter lamps at the gompa, hanging prayer flags and visiting relatives. It is a family and religious festival, not a public show, so visitors should watch respectfully and not expect organised events.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit Lachung during Losar
faqs.a: Yes, if the road is open and your permit is issued. February is snow season, so closures are possible. Some hotels and shops close for a few days, and the village is quieter. Confirm your hotel booking specifically for the Losar dates and keep a buffer day in Gangtok.

faqs.q: Is Losar the same as Losoong
faqs.a: No. Losar is the Tibetan new year, in February or March. Losoong is the Sikkimese new year and harvest festival of the Bhutia community, held on the first day of the eleventh Tibetan month, usually in December, and preceded by masked dances at Phodong and Rumtek.

name: Saga Dawa
when: May–Jun, full moon of the fourth Tibetan month
summary: Saga Dawa marks the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and passing, and the whole fourth Tibetan month is considered holy. In Lachen, prayers are held at Ngodrub Choling monastery, and many Buddhists avoid killing animals and give alms through the month.
body: Saga Dawa is the holiest month of the Tibetan Buddhist year, and its full-moon day, Saga Dawa Duchen, commemorates three events in the Buddha's life: his birth, enlightenment and death or parinirvana. In Sikkim it is a state holiday. In Gangtok, monks carry holy texts from the Tsuklakhang around the town in a large procession that many visitors see.

In Lachen the celebrations are quieter and closer to daily religious life. Families visit the Lachen Monastery, Ngodrub Choling, to light butter lamps and offer prayers, and many people take vows during the month, such as not eating meat or not killing animals. Merit is believed to be multiplied in this month, so alms-giving and circumambulation increase.

Saga Dawa falls in May or June, which is also peak flower season and the start of the monsoon. Lachen was closed to tourists for most of 2023–2026, and pre-monsoon landslides cut North Sikkim roads in late May and June 2025. If you plan around Saga Dawa, check current status before you travel and consider seeing the Gangtok procession as well.
tips: Visit Lachen Monastery in the morning and keep your voice low during prayers.
Respect vows: some families avoid meat this month, so do not push them to share yours.
Build buffer days, since late May and June bring landslide closures.

faqs.a: Saga Dawa is the fourth month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, and its main day is the full moon, usually in late May or June. The exact date changes every year. Sikkim declares a state holiday for it. Check the year's calendar with your operator or Sikkim Tourism.

faqs.q: What happens on Saga Dawa in Sikkim
faqs.a: Buddhists visit monasteries, light butter lamps, make offerings, give alms and often take vows such as avoiding meat. In Gangtok, monks carry sacred texts in a procession from the Tsuklakhang. In villages like Lachen, observances centre on the local monastery and are quieter.

faqs.q: Is Saga Dawa a good time to visit North Sikkim
faqs.a: It can be, if the roads are open. The timing coincides with rhododendron season and the warmest weeks at Gurudongmar, but also with pre-monsoon landslides. Keep the itinerary flexible, add buffer days and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can tourists join Saga Dawa prayers
faqs.a: Visitors may watch and, respectfully, join circumambulation or light a butter lamp at the monastery. Dress modestly, remove shoes before entering prayer halls, walk clockwise and ask before taking photographs. It is a religious observance, so treat it as you would a service in any place of worship.

name: Tendong Lho Rumfaat
summary: Tendong Lho Rumfaat, the Lepcha prayer to Mount Tendong, falls on 8 August and is a Sikkim state holiday. It remembers the mountain that, in Lepcha belief, saved their ancestors from a great flood. In Dzongu it is a day of prayer, gathering and Lepcha dress.
body: According to Lepcha belief, in ancient times a great flood covered the land, and the Lepcha ancestors climbed Tendong Hill, near Namchi in South Sikkim, which rose above the water and saved them. Tendong Lho Rumfaat, meaning the prayer of the Tendong mountain, gives thanks to the mountain as their saviour. It is held on 8 August and is a state holiday in Sikkim.

Lepcha communities across Sikkim, Darjeeling and Kalimpong mark the day with prayers led by Lepcha priests, cultural programmes, traditional dress and food. In Dzongu, the Lepcha reserve, it is a day when villages gather and the old stories are told again, including the folklore of the Teesta and Rangeet rivers that runs through Lepcha culture.

August is monsoon season, and the road to Mangan and Dzongu can be blocked by landslides. If you are in Sikkim on 8 August and want to see the festival, ask your Dzongu homestay well ahead whether a gathering is planned in their area and whether the road is open. Check current status before you travel.
tips: Ask your homestay in advance where the nearest community gathering will be.
Carry rain gear and leech socks; August is the heart of the monsoon.
Ask before photographing prayers or elders in traditional dress.

faqs.a: Tendong Lho Rumfaat is celebrated every year on 8 August, a fixed date, and is a state holiday in Sikkim. Lepcha communities in Sikkim, Darjeeling and Kalimpong mark it with prayers, cultural programmes and traditional dress and food.

faqs.q: What is the story behind Tendong Lho Rumfaat
faqs.a: Lepcha belief holds that during a great flood, their ancestors climbed Tendong Hill near Namchi, which rose above the water and saved them. The festival thanks the mountain as their saviour. It also celebrates the folklore of the Teesta and Rangeet rivers. It is a living tradition of faith.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend Tendong Lho Rumfaat in Dzongu
faqs.a: Visitors staying in Dzongu homestays are often welcome to watch community gatherings respectfully. You need a Dzongu permit, arranged through your homestay. August is monsoon, so roads may be blocked; confirm plans with your hosts and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where else is Tendong Lho Rumfaat celebrated
faqs.a: Across Lepcha communities in Sikkim, including Gangtok and around Tendong Hill near Namchi, and in the Darjeeling and Kalimpong hills of West Bengal. Larger public programmes are often held in towns, while village observances in places like Dzongu are smaller and more personal.

name: Losoong and the Phodong chaam
when: Dec, 28th–29th day of the 10th Tibetan month, then Losoong
summary: Losoong is the Sikkimese new year and harvest festival of the Bhutia community, celebrated by Lepchas as Namsoong. It is preceded by two days of masked chaam dances at Phodong Monastery, an easy, permit-free trip from Gangtok in December.
body: Losoong falls on the first day of the eleventh month of the Tibetan calendar, usually in December, and marks the end of the harvest. It is the traditional new year of the Bhutias, adapted from the rituals of Losar, and Lepchas celebrate it as Namsoong. Families gather, cook and visit friends, and archery and other competitions are held in some places.

Before Losoong, Phodong Monastery holds its annual chaam on the 28th and 29th days of the tenth Tibetan month. Monks in masks and brocade costumes perform sacred dances in the courtyard to drums, cymbals and long horns, depicting stories linked to Guru Padmasambhava and the defeat of evil. Rumtek holds similar dances.

Losoong celebrations often include the burning of an effigy representing a demon king, symbolising the destruction of evil, after offerings of chi, the fermented millet drink, to the gods. Phodong is about 38 km from Gangtok, needs no permit for Indians and is easy to visit for a day. December is dry and clear, though cold in the shade.
tips: Check the chaam dates each year; they follow the Tibetan calendar.
Arrive by mid-morning for a place around the Phodong courtyard.
Do not use flash or walk into the dance area during the chaam.

faqs.q: When is Losoong celebrated in Sikkim
faqs.a: Losoong falls on the first day of the eleventh month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in December. The Phodong Monastery chaam takes place on the 28th and 29th days of the tenth month, just before it. Exact dates change each year, so check once the calendar is published.

faqs.q: Where can I see the Losoong chaam dances
faqs.a: Phodong Monastery, about 38 km north of Gangtok, holds its annual chaam before Losoong, and Rumtek Monastery near Gangtok holds similar dances. Phodong is quieter and needs no permit for Indian citizens. Arrive early on the main day for a good view.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Losoong and Namsoong
faqs.a: They are the same harvest new-year festival seen from two communities. Bhutias call it Losoong, and Lepchas celebrate it as Namsoong. Both mark the end of the harvest season in December, with family gatherings, food, prayers and, in some places, competitions and cultural programmes.

faqs.q: Is December a good time to visit Phodong
faqs.a: Yes. December is dry and clear, with mild sunny days and cold mornings at Phodong, about 1,400 m. The chaam before Losoong is a highlight. It is also snow season further north, so you can combine Phodong with a snow trip to Lachung if permits and roads allow.
